lessons.title: Ordering a drink
lessons.goal: Order coffee, juice and drinks politely.

tip.title: quiero, ¿me pone…?, ¿me da…?
tip.body: In a bar, Spanish speakers are direct: Un café, por favor or Quiero un café, por favor is perfectly polite, as long as you add por favor. In Spain you'll hear ¿Me pone un café? ("Will you put me a coffee?"); in Mexico and elsewhere ¿Me da un café? or ¿Me trae un café?. Juice is zumo in Spain and jugo in Latin America.

lessons.title: The bill, please
lessons.goal: Call the waiter, ask for the bill and pay.

tip.title: camarero, mesero and the tip
tip.body: A waiter is a camarero/camarera in Spain and a mesero/mesera in Mexico and much of Latin America. To call one, just say ¡Disculpe! or ¡Perdone!. The bill only comes when you ask for it. In Spain tipping is small and optional, often just rounding up; in Mexico a tip (propina) of around 10 to 15 percent is customary in restaurants.

lessons.title: Tapas
lessons.goal: Order tapas and raciones to share.

tip.title: tapa, media ración, ración
tip.body: A tapa is a small bite, often eaten standing at the bar with a drink. A ración is a full plate to share, and a media ración is half of one. In some cities, such as Granada, a small tapa often comes free with each drink. Potato is patata in Spain and papa in Latin America.

phrases.note: Fried potatoes with a spicy sauce.

lessons.title: el, la, un, una & plurals
lessons.goal: Use the right article and make nouns plural.

tip.title: Every noun is masculine or feminine
tip.body: Masculine: el café, un bocadillo. Feminine: la cerveza, una tapa. Words in -o are usually masculine and words in -a usually feminine, but learn the article with each noun (el día, la leche). Plural: add -s after a vowel (los cafés, las tapas) and -es after a consonant (el bar → los bares, la ración → las raciones). Unos/unas means "some". Adjectives agree too: el café está bueno, las tapas están buenas.

phrases.note: A bocadillo is a baguette sandwich (Spain); in Mexico a similar sandwich is a torta.

culture.title: Tapas and late meals
culture.body: In Spain, going de tapas means moving from bar to bar with friends, having a drink and a small bite in each. Meals are late: the main meal, la comida, is often eaten around 2 or 3 pm, and dinner, la cena, often not before 9 pm. In Mexico, la comida is also the big meal of the day, in the afternoon, and many people have a lighter dinner. Before eating, people wish each other ¡Buen provecho!, and in Spain also ¡Que aproveche!.
